domain: The practice of oral apprenticeship in traditional craft trades — why 'watch and imitate' teaching is praised as superior to explicit instruction, and what that argument quietly depends on
topic: The practice of oral apprenticeship in traditional craft trades — why 'watch and imitate' teaching is praised as superior to explicit instruction, and what that argument quietly depends on

source.title: Why you should talk to your dead ancestors

movement.gist: Stage the familiar praise of master-apprentice craft learning — 'you cannot teach woodworking or pottery through words, only by watching the master's hands' — as intuitively obvious and widely endorsed by craft revivalists.

Expose that this wordless transmission was never actually wordless: the workshop supplied a constant undercurrent of correction, gossip, naming of tools and errors, and shared judgment among peers that translated the master's movements into learnable distinctions.

Leave unstated the implication that today's revival of 'traditional' craft schools, which restage the master's silent demonstration but not the surrounding community, may be teaching a hollowed-out version of apprenticeship without realizing what's missing.

primary.axis: tacit transmission vs. explicit instruction as the source of craft mastery
poles: mastery is best transmitted through wordless imitation and correction
mastery requires a shared interpretive community to make imitation legible at all

secondary.axis: the apprentice's silence as pedagogical virtue vs. the apprentice's silence as dependence on a vanishing social infrastructure
poles: silence is only possible because a workshop culture supplies the missing commentary

tension_system.interaction: the secondary tension supplies the mechanism (workshop culture as commentary-substitute) that explains why the primary tension cannot simply be resolved in favor of tacit transmission once that culture erodes

family_realization.note: Executes 'Silent Partner' precisely: the assumption that demonstration alone transmits craft is shown to depend invisibly on peer commentary. The erosion—solitary viewers, one-to-one teaching, video abundance—makes the condition visible and asks what remains.

ending_behavior.note: 'Until such groupings exist again somewhere, and they may'—Horizon Clause achieved. Endorses thesis 'until economic conditions return' and refuses consolation. Slight aperture ('genuinely open') prevents absolute closure but suspends endorsement.

voice_consistency.note: Melancholy Realist: accepts hard truths (the revival cannot recover what wasn't designed) without cynicism; explicitly declines comfort ('should not comfort ourselves'). Stubborn particular: the spokeshave angle story. Uneven texture: some sentences abstract, others concrete and muscular.

distractor_efficiency.note: Q1(A): missing_link trap—plausible misdirection from paragraph 1's stated view. Q2(A): level_confusion—'room' could mean building. Q3(B): missing_link—video's arrival seems causal but passage denies it. Q5(B): prior_belief—restates orthodoxy. Q6(D): nec_suff_swap—inverts sufficiency. Strong traps.

explanation_quality.note: Every explanation names passage locations ('Paragraph 2 states explicitly'; 'Paragraph 3 rules out'; 'pre-empting the medium-based fix'). Traps identified by mechanism type, not vagueness. None resort to 'not mentioned.'

answers.reasoning: Text explicitly says commentary came from peers, not the master, sorting motion into distinctions.
Passage identifies loss as the dense peer group generating commentary, not mere space.
Directly follows claim that video changes nothing, blocking footage-as-solution inference.
Anecdote presents appealing claim ('most of us half-believed it') later complicated by talk argument.
Matches passage's synthesis: demonstration and peer commentary were paired; reviving one alone is gesture only.
Argument requires assuming dense peer commentary won't spontaneously emerge in restaged schools.
